title: Modularizing Logistics Orchestration
business: A regional logistics firm managing complex supply chain routing and warehouse inventory.
problem: Tight coupling between database access logic and business rules caused cascading failures whenever the underlying schema changed, leading to high maintenance costs.
solution: Implementing a Layered Architecture organizes responsibilities into ordered layers with controlled dependencies, ensuring the domain logic remains agnostic of data storage details.
steps: Define a Presentation Layer to handle user requests without direct database access.
Establish a Service Layer to coordinate business operations and define the application boundary.
Implement a Domain Layer to encapsulate core business rules and data models.
Create a Data Source Layer to handle persistence, isolating the database schema from the rest of the application.
outcome: Improved maintainability and testability, as changes to the database schema are now confined to the Data Source Layer without impacting business logic.
limitation: A potential limitation is the overhead of mapping data between layers, which can lead to redundant code; this is checked by monitoring the complexity of object transformation logic between the Domain and Data Source layers.

It prevents cascading failures by isolating business rules from data storage.
It increases the speed of database queries.
It reduces the number of UI components required.

questions.question: In Modularizing Logistics Orchestration, what is a key trade-off of the implementation?

The requirement to use a specific database vendor.
The overhead of mapping data between layers.
The inability to perform unit testing.
questions.explanation: Layered architectures often require mapping data between layers, which can introduce redundant code and complexity.
